function.name: telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get
function.description: Retrieves specified telemetry information for a network interface within a given fabric, node, and pod, filtered by the interface and information types. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

fabricName.description: The name of the fabric to limit the nodes pertaining to the given fabric name.

nodeId.description: The identifier of the node to limit the results pertaining to the given node ID.

podId.description: The identifier of the pod to limit the results pertaining to the given pod ID.

interfaceType.description: The type of the interface to limit the results pertaining to the given interface type.

infoType.description: The type of information to retrieve about the interface.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑start guide on how to pull **node‑level** telemetry from a Fabric called *“test‑de”*, when you already know the node’s management IP (`23.31.32.1`).  
I’ll cover both the *CLI* route (the most common way people do this on Arista switches) and the *REST API* route (if your environment exposes the ACI/EAPI endpoints).  

---

### 1️⃣  Identify the Node ID & Pod

Before you can request telemetry, you first need to map the IP address to the internal “Node ID” used by the fabric controller.  
On an Arista switch you can simply log into the console or SSH session and issue:

```bash
$ show interfaces management brief
```

Look for the line whose IPv4 address matches `23.31.32.1`; note the corresponding **NODE-ID** value – e.g., `101`.

If you’re working purely through the API, you could also hit the endpoint:

```
GET https://<controller>/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/interface/mgmt0[ipv4-address='23.31.32.1']
```

but the CLI shortcut above is usually faster.

> ⚠️ If you don’t yet know the node ID, you can discover all nodes in the fabric with:
>
> ```bash
> $ show nodes
> ```
> This will print something like:
>
> ```
> NODE_ID   NAME          STATUS    ROLE     PLATFORM
> ----------------------------------------------------
> 100       sw01.test.de  up        leaf     EOS v5.x
> 101       sw02.test.de  up        spine    EOS v5.x
> ```

Once you’ve got the node ID (say `101`) and you know the pod ID (most single‑pod fabrics default to `1`), you’re ready to fetch telemetry.

---

### 2️⃣  Pull Telemetry Using the Tool Provided

Your tooling layer offers a helper called `telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get`.  
It lets you drill down to a specific interface type on a node inside a fabric.  
Here’s how you’d invoke it for the Ethernet port‑channel that carries the uplink traffic (replace `<tool>` with whatever wrapper you’re using):

```python
from functions import telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get

result = telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get({
    "fabricName": "test-de",
    "nodeId": 101,
    "podId": 1,
    # Pick whichever interface type you care about:
    "interfaceType": "ethernet",      # options: svi|ethernet|loopback|port-channel
    "infoType": "statistics"         # options: interfaces|status|statistics|errors
})

print(result)
```

#### What each parameter means

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `fabricName` | Name of the fabric (“test‑de”). |
| `nodeId` | Numeric ID of the target node (e.g., `101`). |
| `podId` | Usually `1` unless you’re operating across multiple pods. |
| `interfaceType` | Which kind of interface you want stats for. For uplinks, `"port-channel"` is typical. |
| `infoType` | Type of telemetry payload you wish to receive. |

> 📌 **Tip:** If you just want high‑level health metrics, set `infoType="status"`.  
> If you’re troubleshooting packet loss, pick `infoType="errors"`.

---

### 3️⃣  Alternative: Direct REST API Call

If you prefer raw HTTP calls instead of the helper, here’s what the equivalent EAPI request would look like:

```http
GET https://<controller-ip-or-hostname>/api/node/<node-id>/stats/interfaces?fabric=<fabric-name>&pod=<pod-id>

Headers:
Authorization: Basic <base64encoded(username:password)>
Accept: application/json
Content-Type: application/json
```

Replace placeholders as follows:

| Placeholder | Value |
|------------|-------|
| `<controller-ip-or-hostname>` | Your fabric controller’s hostname/IP |
| `<node-id>` | `101` (or whatever you discovered earlier) |
| `<fabric-name>` | `test-de` |
| `<pod-id>` | `1` |

This returns JSON containing counters for all interfaces on that node—exactly what the helper does under the hood.

---

### 4️⃣  Quick Checklist Before You Run Anything

| ✅ Item | Why It Matters |
|---------|----------------|
| Have you logged into the correct fabric? | Avoid pulling wrong data. |
| Know the exact node ID for `23.31.32.1` | The API uses numeric IDs internally. |
| Confirm you have permission to read telemetry | Some environments restrict API access. |
| Verify the interface type exists on that node | Requesting a non‑existent interface yields errors. |

---

### 5️⃣  Sample Output Snapshot

Assuming everything goes well, you’ll get back a structured dictionary similar to:

```json
{
  "interfaces": [
    {
      "name": "Port-Channel10",
      "description": "Uplink to Spine",
      "admin_status": "up",
      "oper_status": "up",
      "speed_mbps": 40000,
      "in_octets": 123456789,
      "out_octets": 987654321,
      ...
    }
  ]
}
```

From there you can parse out error counts, throughput, or feed the data into Grafana dashboards.

---

### 🚀 Wrap‑Up

1. Map `23.31.32.1` → node ID (`101`).  
2. Decide whether you want CLI or API.  
3. Invoke `telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get(...)` (or the raw REST call).  
4. Inspect the returned statistics/status/errors per your needs.

Feel free to let me know if you hit any snags along the way!
